text:
Here is a plain-language version you could send to parents.

---

# Why we are changing how we teach maths

We want to explain an important change in maths lessons.

From now on, we will move away from putting children into different groups based on “ability” and instead teach maths in **mixed-attainment classes**.

We know some parents may feel worried about this. That is understandable. Many parents want to know:

- Will my child still be challenged?
- Will my child still get help if they find maths hard?
- Will this slow some children down?
- Is this really the best way to help children learn?

These are fair questions. We hope this letter helps explain why we are making this change.

---

## What does this mean?

In the past, children may have been placed in “top”, “middle” or “lower” groups for maths.

In mixed-attainment teaching, children of different starting points learn together in the same class.

This does **not** mean teaching everyone exactly the same in exactly the same way.

It means:
- all children study the full maths curriculum
- teachers plan lessons so everyone can take part
- children who need more support get it
- children who are ready to go further are given deeper and more challenging work

---

## Why are we making this change?

### 1. Children can make strong progress in mixed classes

A child’s test score at one moment does not tell us everything they can achieve in the future.

Children learn at different speeds. Some need more time, more practice or a different explanation. If children are placed in lower groups too early, it can be hard for them to catch up later.

Mixed-attainment teaching keeps expectations high for all children.

---

### 2. Grouping by “ability” is not always accurate

No system is perfect at deciding a child’s “ability”.

Children can be placed in groups because of:
- confidence
- how quickly they work
- how well they did on one test
- behaviour
- attendance
- how much support they have had before

These things matter, but they do not always show what a child is capable of learning next.

We do not want children to feel that one label defines them.

---

### 3. Lower groups often get less of the full curriculum

In many schools, when children are placed in lower sets, they are sometimes given easier work for long periods of time. This can mean they miss important ideas and fall further behind.

We want all children to have access to rich, meaningful maths.

Every child should be taught the key ideas they need, not a reduced version of maths.

---

### 4. Children benefit from learning with and from each other

In a mixed class, children hear different ways of thinking.

This can help because:
- explaining an idea helps children understand it better
- hearing a classmate explain something can make maths feel clearer
- children learn that there is more than one way to solve a problem
- discussion builds confidence and understanding

Maths is not only about getting answers quickly. It is also about thinking, explaining and solving problems.

---

### 5. It helps build confidence and belonging

Children can quickly notice who is seen as “good at maths” and who is not.

Being placed in a lower group can affect confidence. Some children begin to think, “I’m just not a maths person.”

We do not believe that maths success belongs only to a small group of children.

We want every child to feel:
- they belong in maths lessons
- they can improve
- effort, practice and good teaching matter
- mistakes are part of learning

---

## Will higher-attaining children still be challenged?

Yes.

This is a very important question.

Challenge does not only mean moving faster onto new topics. It also means:
- solving harder problems
- explaining reasoning
- comparing different methods
- spotting patterns
- proving why something works
- applying maths in unfamiliar situations

Children who grasp ideas quickly will be stretched through deeper thinking, not simply more of the same work.

---

## Will children who struggle get enough help?

Yes.

Children who need extra support will still receive it.

This may include:
- clear step-by-step teaching
- worked examples
- extra practice
- small-group support
- careful checking for understanding
- help from support staff where appropriate
- extra intervention at the right time

The difference is that support will help children succeed with the same important maths ideas as their classmates.

---

## Does this mean the teacher ignores differences between children?

No.

Teachers know children have different strengths and needs.

Mixed-attainment teaching is **not** about pretending all children are the same. It is about teaching in a way that:
- keeps expectations high for everyone
- gives support where needed
- provides challenge where needed
- avoids limiting children too early

---

## What will maths lessons look like?

In lessons, you may see:
- the teacher introducing an idea clearly to the whole class
- visual models and examples to help understanding
- discussion and explanation between pupils
- tasks with different ways in
- questions that make children think deeply
- extra support for some children
- extra challenge for others
- time spent making sure ideas are understood, not rushed

This approach focuses on understanding, not just speed.

---

## Why not keep the current system?

We know setting or streaming can seem simple. Some parents feel it makes sure children are taught at the “right level”.

But in practice, it can create problems:
- children can get stuck in a group that does not reflect their true potential
- lower groups may receive less demanding work
- children’s confidence can be damaged
- movement between groups can be limited
- expectations can become too low for some children

We believe mixed-attainment teaching is a fairer and more ambitious approach.

---

## What do we want for your child?

We want your child to:
- learn the full maths curriculum
- be taught well
- feel confident and included
- be challenged
- get help when needed
- believe they can succeed in maths

This change is about giving every child the best possible chance to do well.

---

## How can parents help?

You do not need to be an expert in maths to help your child.

You can help by:
- asking them to explain what they learned
- praising effort, practice and persistence
- reminding them that it is okay to make mistakes
- encouraging them to keep going when work feels hard
- speaking positively about maths where possible

A powerful message for children is:  
**“You may not understand it yet, but you can learn it.”**

---

## Final message

We understand that changes in school can bring questions and concerns.

This decision has been made carefully because we believe it will help more children succeed in maths, not fewer.

Our aim is not to lower standards.  
Our aim is to raise opportunity, confidence and achievement for all.

If you have questions, we welcome the chance to talk with you.

---

If you want, I can also turn this into:
1. a shorter letter for parents,
2. a FAQ sheet with parent questions and answers, or
3. a speech/script for a parent information evening.
